# Aristotle on Motion, Time, and the Soul's Perceptual Architecture: Toward a Rhetoric of Temporal Dwelling

## 1. Articulating Aristotle's Understanding

Aristotle's philosophical enterprise is fundamentally concerned with the question of how beings show themselves in their being, and it is precisely this concern that renders his thought indispensable for any sustained inquiry into rhetoric, perception, and temporality. Kenneth Burke, in his wide-ranging analysis of dramatistic categories, recognized that the Aristotelian vocabulary of essence, motion, and substance provides a grammar through which the transformations of human motivation can be rendered intelligible; indeed, Burke observed that the logical idea of a thing's essence can be stated in temporal or narrative terms, such that one might define a man's "timeless essence in temporal terms" by attending to origins or endings (Burke, *A Grammar of Motives*, p. 28). This insight—that essence and temporality are intertwined—resonates deeply with the broader Aristotelian project, wherein the study of nature, or physis, is inseparable from the study of motion, change, and the soul's capacity for perception. Thomas Rickert, drawing upon Heidegger's ontological reading of the Greeks, has argued that rhetoric itself must be understood as an emergent result of environmentally situated and interactive engagements, and that to be situated means that "one's emplacement is inseparable from the rhetorical interactions taking place, including material dimensions both within and beyond meaning" (Rickert, *Ambient Rhetoric*, p. 54). Similarly, Daniel Gross, writing in *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, demonstrates that Heidegger's engagement with Aristotle in the 1924 lectures reveals a radical temporality at the heart of rhetorical being, wherein kinesis, or motion, "gives the authentic Da-Charakter to Dasein, the vital place-time of Being" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). Thus, Aristotle's understanding of rhetoric, nature, and the soul cannot be disaggregated; they form a unified field in which motion, perception, and time converge to disclose the character of human dwelling. ## 2. Aristotle on Motion

Motion, or kinesis, occupies a central position in Aristotle's natural philosophy, serving as the ontological hinge upon which his accounts of substance, potentiality, and actuality turn. In the *Metaphysics*, Aristotle develops his understanding of being through a sustained analysis of the categories and their modal determinations, attending to the ways in which beings exist both in potentiality and in actuality; accordingly, the question of motion is never merely physical but always also metaphysical, for it concerns the passage from what a thing can be to what it is (Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, passim). Heidegger's 1924 lectures, as reconstructed in *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, demonstrate that kinesis should not be understood as a Platonic Idea existing beside the world of things but rather as a fundamental way that Dasein is; as Gross reports, Heidegger insisted that "kinesis ist eine Weise des Seins des Daseienden selbst," that is, motion is a mode of the being of that which exists (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 27). 27). The interanimation of activity and passivity in this formulation discloses the middle-voice character of motion that Ned O'Gorman likewise identifies in Aristotle's psychology, where phantasia itself is described as a kind of motion in the soul that mediates between sensation and thought, underlying deliberation and judgment alike (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 4). Hence, motion for Aristotle is not a mere change of place but the very modality through which beings come to presence and disclose themselves. ## 3. Aristotle on Time

Time, in Aristotle's account, is neither a container for events nor a subjective projection but is instead intimately bound to motion and to the soul's capacity for marking distinction and succession. Heidegger, in his *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, explicates the Aristotelian framework by attending to the way in which the study of physis—the study of beings in their self-showing—necessarily entails the study of time as that which accompanies motion. Heidegger observes that Aristotle recognized the fundamental role of the question concerning the "to ti ēn einai," the what-it-was-to-be, and that even the concepts of being-in-the-polis have their foundation in concepts of nature; as Heidegger argues, Aristotle "shifted the weight of his work primarily onto the examination of physis as being" and from there "attained the ground for the study of being as such" (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 177). Time, within this account, is cogiven with kinesis, as Heidegger's analysis of *Physics* Gamma 1 makes clear: the basic topic of the method concerning physis encompasses motion and what is cogiven in it, including the modes of being characterized as dynamis and entelecheia (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, p. 263). The contributors to *Heidegger and Rhetoric*  Heidegger grasps the ontological significance of change and therefore time; specifically, the passions—understood as pathe—are not static knowledge but rather dispositions, Befindlichkeiten, that orient beings temporally within the world (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). Thus, time for Aristotle is not an abstract parameter but something disclosed through the soul's awareness of motion and change, an awareness that is itself structured by perception, passion, and practical engagement. ## 4. The Relation Between Motion and Time

The question of how motion and time relate to one another constitutes one of the most consequential problems in Aristotelian natural philosophy, and it is a question that reverberates through contemporary rhetorical theory. John Bowin has argued that for Aristotle, the perception and cognition of time depend upon the soul's capacity to discriminate between successive states, a capacity that is itself a mode of kinesis; the discriminating power and the time of its exercise must be understood as unified rather than separate, such that time is perceived not in abstraction but through the very motions of the soul as it encounters the world (Bowin, *Aristotle on the Perception and Cognition of Time*, passim). Rickert, extending this insight into the domain of rhetoric, contends that kairos—the opportune moment—must be thought of ambiently, akin to Heidegger's understanding of the Umwelt, the surrounding world, wherein place is "not a neutral, material stage for the emergence of a kairotic situation but itself a complex of relations vitally enmeshed in what comes forth to take place as kairos" (Rickert, *Ambient Rhetoric*, p. 109). Burke, for his part, recognized that the temporalizing of essence—the translation of logical priority into temporal or narrative sequence—serves as one of the fundamental operations of human motivation, and that one may state essence in terms of beginnings or endings, origins or fruitions (Burke, *A Grammar of Motives*, p. 28). What emerges from these converging perspectives is that motion and time are not two separable phenomena but rather co-constitutive dimensions of the soul's engagement with the world; indeed, the soul does not first perceive motion and then infer time, but rather perceives motion as temporal, disclosing the before and after that constitute time's very structure. ## 5. Aisthēsis and Temporal Awareness

Perception, or aisthēsis, furnishes the primary ground upon which temporal awareness is built, and it does so not as a passive reception of stimuli but as an active, embodied engagement with the world. The contributors to *Heidegger and Rhetoric* note that for Heidegger's Aristotle, fear—phobos—is paradigmatic of temporal perception: it becomes present not through direct experience, aisthēsis, but through phantasia, and the semeia, or signs, furnish "the Da-Charakter of fear" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). This analysis reveals that aisthēsis is not merely the registration of present stimuli but is always already oriented toward future and past, shaped by dispositions and passions that themselves constitute modes of being-in-the-world. Heidegger observes that Aristotle's account of the passion of fear reveals a great sensitivity to temporal dimensions of affect, noting that the tense of fear is future, its voice subjunctive, and its mode the possible (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). Burke, in his account of rhetorical identification, similarly recognizes that the transformation of motivational principles—whether through imagery of life and death, or through the narrative temporalization of essence—depends upon the capacity of the perceiver to inhabit temporal horizons that extend beyond the immediate present; the imagery of transformation is, he argues, "limited only by the imagination and ingenuity of poets," yet shaped by the selective pressures of existence that favor certain images above others (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, p. 27). Thus, aisthēsis is always already temporal, oriented not merely to what is but to what has been and what may come, and it is this orientation that makes rhetorical persuasion—and indeed all practical deliberation—possible. ## 6. Phantasia and Temporal Unification

Phantasia, as Aristotle develops it in *De Anima* and as it reverberates through the *Rhetoric*, serves as the faculty that unifies the disparate moments of temporal experience into a coherent field of appearance. O'Gorman, in his careful analysis, demonstrates that phantasia is a distinct part of the psyche, essential to all animal action and all human thought, including deliberation, contemplation, and creativity; it "underlies and mediates between sense perception and the mind" (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 4). What is critical here is that phantasia is not merely reproductive but productive: it generates images that persist beyond immediate sensation, furnishing the "after-images" and residues of sense perception that allow the soul to compare, deliberate, and judge across temporal intervals. O'Gorman  Aristotle describes a phantasmatic mental activity as bouleutikē, designating deliberation as entailing "the combination of mental images" (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 4). This deliberative phantasia is precisely what enables the rhetorical situation to cohere: the orator, through lexis understood as phantasia, makes appearances present to the audience in a manner that is, as Aristotle states, "appearance and is for the audience" (O'Gorman, *Aristotle's Phantasia in the Rhetoric*, p. 4). The contributors to *Heidegger and Rhetoric* reinforce this point by observing that fear itself operates through phantasmata—mental pictures of future evil—rather than through direct sensation, and that these phantasmata furnish the temporal structure of affective response (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 115). Burke's analysis of the ritualistic transformation of traits through imagery similarly depends upon the capacity of phantasia to hold together past experience, present motivation, and future possibility within a unified dramatic frame (Burke, *A Rhetoric of Motives*, pp. 27–28). Accordingly, phantasia is not a secondary or derivative faculty but the very condition for temporal unification, enabling the soul to dwell within time rather than merely pass through it. ## 7. Heidegger's Interpretation of Aristotle

Heidegger's reading of Aristotle, developed most extensively in the 1924 summer semester lectures and subsequently in *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, constitutes a decisive reorientation of the Aristotelian legacy. Heidegger insists that the Greek understanding of being is fundamentally an understanding of being as presence, Anwesenheit, and that the study of motion and time in the *Physics* and *Metaphysics* is the ground from which all subsequent ontology proceeds. In *Basic Concepts*, Heidegger demonstrates that science is "a matter of the correct relationship to the matters" and that researchers such as Empedocles and Democritus were "led by truth itself" and "borne by the matter itself" toward genuine insight into the being of beings (Heidegger, *Basic Concepts of Aristotelian Philosophy*, pp. 176–177). This insistence on the priority of the matter—the pragma—over theoretical preconception is what distinguishes Heidegger's Aristotle from the scholastic tradition. Furthermore, Heidegger's analysis of kinesis, as discussed in *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, reveals that the complex relationship between pathēsis and poiētikos, whose interanimation defines motion, "reaches into the true center of the Greek view of the world and life" (Multiple Authors, *Heidegger and Rhetoric*, p. 27). Bowin's analysis of temporal cognition extends this framework by showing that for Aristotle the perception of time requires a unity of the discriminating power and the occasion of its exercise, a unity that Heidegger would characterize as the ecstatic temporality of Dasein (Bowin, *Aristotle on the Perception and Cognition of Time*, passim). What Heidegger ultimately discloses is that Aristotle's philosophy of motion and time is not a predecessor to modern physics but rather an ontological inquiry into the conditions under which beings show themselves as they are—an inquiry that remains indispensable for any rhetoric attentive to the temporal, perceptual, and affective dimensions of human dwelling in the world. ---
